prompt.context: Our client, Pill Pushers, sells generic prescription drugs in the US. It has been relatively successful over the past several years and has products in most of the chain retail pharmacies. Pill Pushers just received a proposed price schedule for various drugs from its Indian manufacturing partner and has asked for our recommendation on which 1 or 2 drugs to produce.
prompt.question: How do we arrive at a recommendation on which 1 or 2 drugs Pill Pushers should add to its product mix?

clarifying_info.q: Does the client sell outside the US?
Does the client manufacture its own drugs?
clarifying_info.a: Mostly, the client outsources manufacturing but keeps marketing and distribution in-house.

clarifying_info.q: What types of drugs does the client sell?
clarifying_info.a: Generic prescription drugs only — no over-the-counter drugs like aspirin or ibuprofen, and no patented branded drugs like Viagra or Lipitor. Doctors are important customers.

exhibits.title: Proposed Price Schedule
exhibits.shows: A table listing 10 drugs (numbered 1-10) across four practice areas (Psychiatry, Dermatology, Cardiology, Oncology) with columns for Retail Price per Bottle, Number of Pills per Bottle, and Percent Distribution Cost per Pill.
exhibits.data: Drug 1 Psychiatry $9.00/bottle 45 pills 50% dist; Drug 2 Dermatology $19.50/bottle 65 pills 70% dist; Drug 3 Cardiology $6.40/bottle 40 pills 50% dist; Drug 4 Oncology $15.00/bottle 60 pills 40% dist; Drug 5 Psychiatry $8.00/bottle 40 pills 25% dist; Drug 6 Dermatology $8.25/bottle 55 pills 60% dist; Drug 7 Cardiology $14.00/bottle 70 pills 70% dist; Drug 8 Oncology $10.00/bottle 50 pills 30% dist; Drug 9 Psychiatry $12.50/bottle 50 pills 40% dist; Drug 10 Oncology $8.00/bottle 40 pills 50% dist

exhibits.title: Sales Division
exhibits.shows: A table showing the Sales Division broken down by practice area (Psychiatry, Dermatology, Cardiology, Oncology) with rows for Number of Salespeople, Products per Salesperson, and Fixed Costs per Employee.
exhibits.data: Psychiatry: 42 salespeople, 5 products/person, $60,000 fixed cost/employee; Dermatology: 34 salespeople, 4 products/person, $70,000 fixed cost/employee; Cardiology: 29 salespeople, 2 products/person, $50,000 fixed cost/employee; Oncology: 47 salespeople, 3 products/person, $50,000 fixed cost/employee

exhibits.title: Salesman Performance
exhibits.shows: A table showing how a salesman's total sell volume changes as the number of products they sell increases from 1 to 6.
exhibits.data: 1 product: sell volume 100; 2 products: 170; 3 products: 220; 4 products: 260; 5 products: 290; 6 products: 260

framework: Customers by pill: market size and growth, frequency and duration of usage (chronic vs. acute), role of non-users (doctors, pharmacies, insurers), decision power and prescribing process

Competitors by pill: number, revenues, profits, trends; product types (pills, patches, liquids); branded vs. generic; positioning and pricing; barriers to entry/exit; distribution access; competitive response
Collaborators by pill: identify key collaborators (pharmacies, doctors, Indian manufacturer); objectives of each (profit, market share, diversification)
Company: objective (profit, market share, diversification); current product mix and ease of adding new products; big-picture strategy (exit, long-term plan, contingencies, next steps)

questions.prompt: Question 1: How should we evaluate the proposed price schedule? (Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: The key insight is that the price schedule mixes units — some figures are per bottle and some are per pill — so the candidate must convert everything to a common unit (price per pill). Revenue per pill = (Retail Price / # Pills) x (1 - % Distribution Cost). Volumes are assumed equal across pills (not bottles). After conversion, Oncology and Psychiatry drugs all yield > $0.10 revenue per pill, while Dermatology and Cardiology drugs yield < $0.10 revenue per pill. This eliminates Dermatology and Cardiology. Bonus insight: not all pills are equal in real-world volume or usage (chronic daily pills vs. acute short-course pills).

math.setup: Revenue per pill = (Retail Price per Bottle / # Pills per Bottle) x (1 - % Distribution Cost per Pill). Apply to each of the 10 drugs.
steps: Conclusion: Oncology drugs (4, 8, 10) and Psychiatry drugs (1, 5, 9) all have rev/pill >= $0.10; Dermatology (2, 6) and Cardiology (3, 7) have rev/pill < $0.10 — eliminate them
math.answer: Dermatology and Cardiology drugs are less profitable per pill. Narrow the choice to Oncology and Psychiatry drugs.

questions.prompt: Question 2: How do features of the Sales Division affect the recommendation? (Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: The key insight is salesman brain capacity. A salesman can talk about at most 5 drugs (capacity = 5 products per person). Psychiatry salesmen already sell 5 products each — they are at full capacity. Adding a Psychiatry drug requires hiring new salespeople, incurring fixed training costs. Oncology salesmen currently sell 3 products each — they have room for 2 more drugs at zero additional fixed cost. This eliminates Psychiatry drugs and points to Oncology. The fixed cost calculation for adding a Psychiatry drug: 42 salespeople x $60,000 training/salesperson = $2.52 million in additional fixed costs. Oncology has no such fixed cost for adding up to 2 more drugs.

math.setup: If a new Psychiatry drug is added, new salespeople must be hired because existing ones are at capacity (5 products each). Fixed cost = # Psychiatry salespeople x training cost per salesperson.
steps: Psychiatry salespeople: 42; Training cost per salesperson: $60,000
Fixed cost of adding Psychiatry drug: 42 x $60,000 = $2,520,000
Oncology salespeople currently sell 3 products each; capacity is 5; room for 2 more drugs with zero added fixed cost
Fixed cost of adding Oncology drug (up to 2): $0
math.answer: Adding a Psychiatry drug costs $2.52 million in fixed salesperson training costs; adding an Oncology drug (up to 2 additional) costs nothing in fixed costs.

questions.prompt: Bonus Question: What does Exhibit 3 reveal about salesman performance?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 (provided only if the candidate raises the idea that a salesman can only remember a limited number of things) shows that total sell volume peaks at 5 products (290) and falls at 6 products (260). This confirms the capacity constraint of 5 products per salesman. The marginal volume added by the 6th product is negative (-30), meaning adding beyond capacity actively reduces performance. Important: 1 customer sees only 1 salesman, so splitting the portfolio across multiple low-product specialists is not viable.

math.setup: Marginal sell volume = sell volume at N products minus sell volume at N-1 products.
math.answer: Maximum effective capacity is 5 products per salesman; the 6th product reduces total output.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors might affect the recommendation or should be explored further?

categories.name: Manufacturing & Supply
ideas: Other Indian or international manufacturers may offer better price schedules
Quality and reliability of the Indian manufacturer
Lead times and supply chain risk

categories.name: Sales Force
ideas: Sales training program efficiency — could improve capacity beyond 5 products per salesman
Whether salespeople across divisions could cross-sell
Incentive structure of the sales force

categories.name: Market & Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Market size and growth rate for Oncology drugs
Number and strength of generic competitors in Oncology
Patent cliff timing for branded Oncology drugs creating generic opportunity

categories.name: Regulatory & Risk
ideas: FDA approval requirements for new generic drugs
Reimbursement and formulary positioning with insurers

recommendation: Recommend adding Drugs #4 and #8 (Oncology drugs) to the current product mix — they have the highest revenue per pill ($0.15 and $0.14 respectively) and the lowest incremental fixed cost (zero, because Oncology salespeople currently handle only 3 products and have capacity for 2 more)
Oncology drugs dominate on both dimensions: higher profitability than Cardiology and Dermatology, and no new fixed sales costs unlike Psychiatry
risks: Other manufacturers may offer better price schedules — the current Indian partner's pricing should be benchmarked
The Sales Division's training program may not be optimal — current 5-product capacity could potentially be expanded
Real-world pill volumes are not equal (chronic vs. acute conditions); if volume assumptions change, the ranking could shift
next_steps: Benchmark the Indian manufacturer's pricing against other potential manufacturing partners
Review the Sales Division's training program to explore whether salesman capacity can be increased beyond 5 products
Validate equal-volume assumption against actual prescription data for Oncology drugs
